2.text: Ceremonial connected with the Killing of Wild Reindeer-Bucks. — Of

3.text: all animals killed on the hunt, the Reindeer Chukchee set the highest value

4.text: on wild reindeer-bucks killed in the herd during the rutting-season, because

5.text: their coming is thought to affect favorably the fortune of the herd.¹ With
5.note: Body footnote reference; machine text read the superscript 1 as a close-bracket. Superscript sort U+00B9 keyed tight against the period per §2.10.

6.text: the killing of such bucks a complicated ceremonial — performed late in the

7.text: fall, after the rutting-season is over — is connected. The Chukchee contend

8.text: that these animals are not hunted down by the personal skill of the hunter,

9.text: but that they are lured within his easy reach by the influence of the herd,

10.text: therefore it is only fitting that a return should be made in the form of a

11.text: ceremonial and sacrifice; while, on the other hand, animals killed far from

12.text: home and herd require no such ceremony.

13.text: Since the ceremonial connected with the hunt of walrus and larger kinds

14.text: of seal is performed about the same season and with somewhat similar details

15.text: by both the Maritime Chukchee and the Asiatic Eskimo, it is my opinion that

16.text: the purpose of this ceremonial is to celebrate success on the hunt. I believe

17.text: it is connected with the bucks killed in the herd simply because they represent

18.text: among the Reindeer Chukchee the most important game hunted. With the

19.text: Reindeer Chukchee the ceremonial has a special name, ênatčɪˊɪrg̣ɪn. The
19.resolved: ê = e+U+0302; č = c+U+030C; ɪ = U+026A (x3, before stress, and twice in the -ɪrg̣ɪn suffix); ˊ = U+02CA stress, postposed to the first ɪ; g̣ = g+U+0323
19.note: Tier-1 form, unglossed, no lexicon match (below the two-page floor). Read at 4x: after č a bare dotless stem (ɪ, not r — no shoulder), then the stress mark, then ɪrgɪn where the g carries a separate dot below distinct from its tail loop, matching the -tɪrg̣ɪn/-ɪrg̣ɪt suffix pattern attested elsewhere in the lexicon (qaanmaˊtɪrg̣ɪn, Yaˊtirg̣ɪn). Machine text read č as é, the first ɪ as r, and the stress mark as an apostrophe.

20.text: Maritime Chukchee call the ceremonial connected with walrus-hunting by this

21.text: name; and the Maritime Koryak apply it, with the proper phonetic change,

22.text: to the ceremonial of the whale.

23.text: The details of the ceremonial with the Reindeer Chukchee are as follows.

24.text: The first wild buck that comes to the herd is frequently met with incantations,

25.text: the purpose of which is to make him assume for a while the ways of domes-

26.text: ticated reindeer, so that he may serve as a successful breeder. The details

27.text: of the incantations will be described later in a special chapter. After a week

28.text: or ten days, when the incantations have lost their power, the owner of the

29.text: herd catches the buck with his lasso and throws him down on a piece of the
29.note: A speck sits above the d of "herd" in the composite; read as ink dust, not a diacritic — the word carries no licensed mark and is ordinary English.

30.text: tent-covering. Then a young female, which is to represent his wife, is caught

31.text: and thrown down by his side. The mistress puts on her overcoat, and,

32.text: holding the buck’s head in her lap, covers it with her overcoat. The master

33.text: now stabs the buck with an antler knife made for this purpose; then he stabs

34.text: the female with an ordinary iron knife. After that a little urine in a chamber-

35.text: vessel is offered to the buck while he is still in the agonies of death. With

36.text: the handle of the antler knife, fashioned like a spatula, the owner of the herd

37.text: touches all parts of the carcass of the animal, thus taking back his incantation,

38.text: and restoring the buck to his freedom. As long as the buck is under the

39.text: influence of the spell, the master must abstain from untying knots, otherwise
